## 1. Window / trigger / lateness specification

```java
// Flink-style declarative spec
Window:  TUMBLE(event_time, INTERVAL '2' MINUTE)          // epoch-aligned, [00:00, 00:02), [00:02, 00:04), …
Trigger: EventTimeTrigger(WM >= window_end)               // exactly one ON-TIME pane
         + late-element re-fire (after ON-TIME pane, WM < end + allowed_lateness)
         + FINAL at (WM >= end + allowed_lateness) | end-of-input
         [early/periodic panes disabled for this replay]
AllowedLateness: 5 minutes  → state retained until end + 5min, GCs at that point
Accumulation:   ACCUMULATING_AND_RETRACTING  → each pane is the FULL window sum;
                downstream must retract the prior pane for that window before applying the new one
Watermark:      max(event_time seen) - 30s  (monotonically non-decreasing)
```

Two knobs matter and they are **independent**: `WM_DELAY = 30s` decides when the *first* pane fires; `ALLOWED_LATENESS = 5min` decides how long after that a window can still absorb corrections. My earlier changelog also said `allowed_lateness = 2h` — that was written for a 1-hour window on a production stream; for this 10-minute toy I'm using 5 minutes as you specified, so the two are simply different deployments of the same contract.

## 2. Pane emissions (from the run)

| at | window | pane | kind | value | elements |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 00:00–00:02 | 1 | ON-TIME | +10.00 | evt-001 |
| 3 | 00:02–00:04 | 1 | ON-TIME | +7.25 | evt-003 |
| **4** | 00:00–00:02 | **2** | **LATE (retract+update)** | **+35.50** | evt-001, evt-002 |
| **7** | 00:02–00:04 | **2** | **LATE (retract+update)** | **+19.25** | evt-003, evt-004 |
| 8 | 00:00–00:02 | 2 | FINAL | +35.50 | evt-001, evt-002 |
| 8 | 00:04–00:06 | 1 | ON-TIME | +4.99 | evt-005 |
| 8 | 00:06–00:08 | 1 | ON-TIME | −10.00 | evt-007 |
| 9 | 00:04–00:06 | 2 | LATE (retract+update) | +13.74 | evt-005, evt-006 |
| 10 | 00:06–00:08 | 2 | LATE (retract+update) | −6.50 | evt-007, evt-009 |
| 11 | 00:02–00:04 | 2 | FINAL | +19.25 | evt-003, evt-004 |
| 12 | 00:06–00:08 | 3 | LATE (retract+update) | +8.50 | evt-007, evt-009, evt-008 |
| EOI | 00:04–00:06 | 2 | FINAL | +13.74 | evt-005, evt-006 |
| EOI | 00:06–00:08 | 3 | FINAL | +8.50 | evt-007, evt-009, evt-008 |
| EOI | 00:08–00:10 | 1 | ON-TIME | +27.50 | evt-010, evt-011 |
| EOI | 00:08–00:10 | 1 | FINAL | +27.50 | evt-010, evt-011 |

Five windows, final sums `35.50 / 19.25 / 13.74 / 8.50 / 27.50 = 104.49` — matching the deduped grand total from the previous step.

## 3. How panes are emitted, and how late data revises them

**The root cause of almost all the revision traffic is a single watermark jump.** At arrival 3, `evt-007` carries `event_time = 00:06:00`, which rockets the max event time from `00:02:00` to `00:06:00` and the watermark from `00:01:30` to `00:05:30`. That instantly satisfies `WM >= window_end` for **two** windows at once — `[00:00, 00:02)` and `[00:02, 00:04)` — so both fire *speculatively* with whatever they happen to hold (`+10.00` and `+7.25`). Every element for those windows still in flight (`evt-002`, `evt-004`) then lands *after* publication and forces a revision. This is precisely the bounded-out-of-orderness trade-off: a wider `WM_DELAY` would have delayed those first panes and produced fewer, cleaner revisions, at the cost of higher result latency.

**Panes are full-state snapshots, not deltas.** Because accumulation is `ACCUMULATING_AND_RETRACTING`, pane 2 of `[00:00, 00:02)` is `+35.50`, not the `+25.50` increment from `evt-002`. A downstream consumer must interpret pane *n* as a **retraction of pane n−1 plus an assertion of pane n**; it cannot simply `SUM()` the panes, or it would double-count. In Flink's `Row` this is the `RowKind.UPDATE_BEFORE` / `UPDATE_AFTER` pair.

**Not every behind-watermark element is a late-data revision.** Arrivals 2 (`evt-001`) and 5 (`evt-005`) both have `event_time < watermark`, yet their windows had not yet fired, so they were simply buffered — no correction needed. Lateness is a property of *the window relative to the watermark*, not of the element alone. Only arrivals 4, 7, 9, 10, 12 hit an already-fired window.

**The `evt-007` correction behaves correctly under revision.** Window `[00:06, 00:08)` is born from a negative element, so its very first ON-TIME pane is `−10.00`. It then absorbs `evt-009` (`+3.50` → `−6.50`) and `evt-008` (`+15.00` → `+8.50`). Each step emits a retract-and-replace pair; the intermediate `−6.50` is visible to downstream but transient. This is what "correction as a new event" costs you on the read side: the ledger is eventually correct, but a live dashboard will briefly show a negative revenue for that window.

**Where FINAL comes from.** Two windows reached their allowed-lateness deadline naturally — `[00:00, 00:02)` (end + 5min = 00:07, crossed at arrival 8) and `[00:02, 00:04)` (00:09, crossed at arrival 11) — and their state was GC'd, emitting a pane marked final. The other two (`[00:04, 00:06)`, `[00:06, 00:08)`) have deadlines of 00:11 and 00:13 that the stream never reaches, so they only flush at end-of-input. **That distinction matters operationally**: windows closed by the watermark deadline are safe to delete; windows flushed at EOI are closed only because the source ended, and if the job restarts into the same window they would reopen. There is no end-of-stream marker in this contract, so EOI is an operational event, not a data event.

**One thing to flag:** the duplicate `evt-001` at arrival 6 never appears in the arrival log, because I applied `event_id` dedup *before* the streaming simulation. That is the correct placement — de-duplicating inside the window operator would make pane values depend on arrival ordering — but it means the windowing layer sees 11 events, not 12, and any per-pane element counts (`n_elems`) you read above are post-dedup.
